About the Project

Predicting a missing word in one Polynesian language from its relatives in the others.

Overview

This project is an end-to-end pipeline that takes in Polynesian language data and predicts missing words. We used a sequence-to-sequence machine learning model for the language prediction. The whole project is written in Python, with the PyTorch library used for the model and pandas used for data cleaning.

Polynesian languages descend from a common ancestor, so related words change in regular ways from one language to the next. Hawaiian make ("to die") corresponds to Māori, Samoan, and Tongan mate, because Hawaiian k regularly matches t in the others. Given the words for one meaning in some of the languages, the model predicts the word in a language where it's hidden.

Data

Our data comes from the Austronesian Comparative Dictionary (ACD), which groups related words across languages into cognate sets. We used six languages: Hawaiian, Māori, Rarotongan, Samoan, Tahitian, and Tongan.

Cleaning took the 2,981 recorded forms in those languages down to 562 usable cognate sets:

  • Removed loanwords, which don't follow the regular sound changes.
  • Kept only words that belong to a cognate set, and only sets with at least two of the languages.
  • Standardized spelling (glottal stops as ʔ, long vowels with macrons, Māori wh as f), and removed affixes and multi-word phrases.
  • Kept one word per language per set, and collapsed repeated forms such as ʔioʔio when a related language has the single form.

Each cognate set gives one example per language: hide that language's word and predict it from the rest. That makes 1,822 examples, split into training, validation, and test sets. Related cognate sets that share a root always land in the same split, so the model is never tested on a near-copy of something it trained on.

The ACD has only two usable Tahitian words, so Tahitian isn't offered as a target here. We also experimented with the Austronesian Basic Vocabulary Database (ABVD), which has far more Tahitian, as extra training data.

Model

The model reads and writes words one character at a time. Its input is the target language plus each available related word, tagged with its language. An encoder (a bidirectional GRU) reads those characters, and a decoder (another GRU) writes the missing word letter by letter. At each step, attention lets the decoder focus on the matching characters in the inputs, which is how it learns correspondences like Hawaiian k → Māori t without being told them.

During training we randomly hide and reorder the related languages, so the model learns to work from whatever words are available. Training stops when its character error on the validation set stops improving.

The demo uses an ensemble of three models trained with different random seeds. At each letter it averages their predictions and uses beam search to keep the five most likely partial words. The top result is the prediction, and the rest are shown as ranked alternatives. Each candidate's confidence score is its average per-letter probability, so the scores don't add up to 1.

The "Why this prediction?" text is drawn from sound correspondences found in the training data. It describes evidence that supports the answer, not the model's internal reasoning.

Results

We compare the model against two simple baselines:

  • Copy: take the word from the most similar related language.
  • Mapped: copy the word, but first apply the most common character substitutions learned from the training data.

Results on the 212 validation examples:

MethodExact matchAvg. character error
Copy baseline45.3%21.2%
Mapped baseline77.8%9.7%
Single model (average of 3)76.4%9.4%
Ensemble of 3, beam search77.4%8.8%

"Avg. character error" is edit distance divided by word length: the share of characters that are wrong. The ensemble ties the mapped baseline on exact matches and is closer when it misses. The correct word is in its top three guesses 84.9% of the time.

The model is strongest on Māori (88% exact) and weakest on Tongan (61%, below the baseline's 69%). Tongan kept a glottal stop and an h that most of the other languages lost, so the related words often don't show where they belong. Most other errors are near misses: about half are off by a single character. The model also tends to cut long or repeated words short, for example kapakapa → kapaka.
